brief:
Our grain co-op's weighbridge at the Dunmore Road elevator backs up every harvest and I have to decide how we rebuild intake scheduling before September. Right now it's first come, first served and the drivers hate it. Below is yesterday's arrivals log, pasted straight from the scale software. I want you to come up with at least three genuinely different ways we could fix this (not three flavours of the same idea), replay yesterday's queue under each one, and let me compare them against each other on wait time, driver effort, and what we'd have to build or buy. The Tuesday to Thursday rush is what I care most about.

We're a six-year-old craft brewery and the labels look it. I want to see several quite different visual directions for the whole range at once, applied to our real beers (not lorem ipsum), so I can put them next to each other and pick one or steal pieces from each. Hard constraints: ABV has to stay legible from arm's length on shelf, the two seasonals need to stand out from the core range, and the pun names must not get cropped. Please propose at least three directions that really differ in mood, not just in colour, and apply each to everything below. Notes are from the sales team and the head brewer.

I need a pull request description for the branch below, which reworks how our library system syncs the catalogue to the branch kiosks. Reviewers on our team are busy and skeptical; the last description for something this size got "what am I looking at?" as its only comment. Give them what they need: why we did it, what actually changed grouped in a way that makes sense (not just a commit dump), what's risky, what they should check first, and what was deliberately left out. Commit log and the CI result are pasted from the branch.

The integration failure is test_resume_after_partial_apply, which fails about 1 run in 10 on main as well. Rollout plan: Eastgate first, the other 11 branches after a week. Rollback means setting the cursor back to null and a full resync, about 9 minutes per kiosk.

I'm reviewing a pull request on our pharmacy system tonight and I'm out of my depth in the dosing code. The change moves how paediatric doses are rounded before they're sent to the infusion pumps. I don't have long. Help me review it: what the change is really doing, which files deserve my real attention versus a skim, where a mistake could hurt a patient, and what questions I should be asking the author. File list with the author's notes and the comments so far are below; blank means nobody has said anything.

src/dosing/bands.ts | +30 / -12 | weight bands now 0-3 kg, 3-10 kg, 10-25 kg, 25+ kg | 
src/dosing/limits.ts | +9 / -4 | max mg/kg/day cap, now per-drug | 
src/pump/export.ts | +52 / -20 | send mL/h with 1 decimal (was 2) | Tomasz: "pump firmware accepts 2, are we sure?"
src/pump/units.ts | +14 / -0 | mcg to mg helpers | 
test/dosing/round.test.ts | +260 / -35 | 48 new cases | 
test/dosing/fixtures/gentamicin.json | +1,120 / -0 | generated from the formulary | nobody has read this one
test/pump/export.test.ts | +71 / -9 | |

The change touches 11 files, 1,698 lines added and 144 removed. Checks are green. Release is Thursday, and the ward champion at St. Brendan's Children's wants a summary before then. I'm a developer, not a clinician, so explain the clinical bits plainly.

I run the front-end for a youth football league's live scores. The goal-scored moment is flat and people miss it; I want to prototype how the score change should feel and tune it until it's right, then hand the final numbers back to me. Below are the states and timings the current spec has, with the comments from the product owner and the designer. I'd like to see them play, change durations and easing myself, and see how the whole sequence of them runs together (a goal followed by a red card 20 seconds later is the case I worry about). Include the real numbers for a plausible match: Riverside U14 vs St. Catherine's, 2-1.

event | duration (ms) | easing | notes
score digit roll | 420 | ease-out | slow? Dev says it feels sluggish on old phones
goal flash behind team name | 900 | linear | must not trigger photosensitive warnings (max 3 flashes/sec)
scorer name slide-in | 350 | cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1) | "Mbeki, 23'" etc; names with apostrophes truncate badly
scorer name hold | 4,000 | n/a | 
scorer name slide-out | 250 | ease-in | 
red card drop | 600 | ease-in-out | designer wants a small bounce
substitution swap arrows | 500 | ease-in-out | 
half-time banner | 800 | ease-out | 
full-time confetti | 2,500 | | only if the home team wins; product owner unsure
VAR check pulse | 1,200 | ease-in-out | loops until decision, then stops; "stop it politely"
connection lost fade | 300 | ease-out | 
stale data warning (after 15 s) | 200 | | amber, never red
tab refocus catch-up | 0 | | jumps to current score with no animation; some say it should still animate

Constraints: the whole goal sequence has to finish inside 6 seconds, the score digits must stay readable the entire time, and there is a reduced-motion setting where almost everything should just be an instant change. Games are watched mostly on phones, often by parents standing on a touchline in glare.

I'm a project coordinator at a city's public works department. Council keeps asking why a basic sidewalk-repair permit takes so long, and I need something I can show them that explains how an application actually moves through our office, step by step, and where it gets stuck. Data below is from the permit system for the last quarter (1,846 applications) with the notes our staff put in. Please make it something a councillor with 3 minutes can follow, and also something I can hand to the department head to argue for fixing the worst step. Note that some applications loop back, and some skip steps.

step | owner | median days | % of applications reaching it | notes
1 Application received | Front counter | 0 | 100 | online and paper, paper gets keyed in late
2 Completeness check | Permit clerks | 2 | 100 | 31% bounced back to applicant (missing site plan, usually)
3 Applicant resubmits | Applicant | 9 | 31 | longest wait we don't control
4 Utility locate request | Engineering (Dana's team) | 4 | 88 | gas and telecom reply separately
5 Utility replies collected | Engineering | 11 | 88 | "waiting on the phone company" is in 140 notes
6 Street-use review | Traffic & Transportation | 3 | 64 | only if lane or sidewalk closure
7 Tree and root check | Parks (forestry) | 6 | 27 | triggered inside 3 m of a city tree
8 Heritage district review | Planning, Heritage Sub-committee | 21 | 9 | meets monthly; miss a meeting, add 4 weeks
9 Fee calculation | Finance | 1 | 97 | fees range $85 to $1,240
10 Payment | Applicant | 3 | 97 | 6% pay late
11 Final approval and signature | Director of Works | 2 | 94 | signs on Tuesdays and Fridays
12 Permit issued | Permit clerks | 1 | 94 | 
13 Rejected or withdrawn | n/a | n/a | 6 | most are withdrawn after the heritage step

Overall median time from received to issued: 29 days. Target in the service charter: 15 working days. Fastest 10% finish in 8 days, slowest 10% take 71 days or more. Staffing: 4 permit clerks, 2 engineers shared with other work, 1 director.

I'm a crew scheduling analyst at a regional airline and I have to change the crew-rostering rules file for the winter schedule. It's a long list of settings that someone could easily break (last year a typo in a rest rule got us a regulator query). I don't want to edit it by hand in a text editor. I want to be able to change the values safely, with the limits enforced, a clear flag when two settings contradict each other, and a way to see what I changed compared with what's live. Then give me the edited settings back in exactly this same layout so it drops into the repo. The limits in the comments are from the regulator and our union agreement; the first number in a comment is the minimum allowed and the second the maximum.

# crew rules, regional fleet (Q4)
duty.max_hours_domestic = 13.0   # allowed 8-13, regulator
duty.max_hours_extended = 14.5   # allowed 13-15, needs captain's discretion flag
rest.min_hours_home_base = 11    # allowed 10-24, regulator
rest.min_hours_layover = 10      # allowed 9-24; must not exceed rest.min_hours_home_base
rest.weekly_hours = 36           # allowed 30-72, union agreement, was 34 until 2025
flight.max_sectors_per_duty = 6  # allowed 1-8
flight.max_block_hours_28d = 100 # allowed 60-100, regulator
flight.max_block_hours_365d = 1000 # allowed 800-1,000, regulator
reserve.callout_notice_min = 90  # minutes, allowed 60-240, union
reserve.max_consecutive_days = 5 # allowed 1-7
reserve.airport_standby_hours = 4  # allowed 0-8; counts toward duty
swap.window_hours_before = 48    # allowed 12-168
swap.allow_cross_fleet = false   # true or false; only true if training.cross_fleet_ok is true
training.cross_fleet_ok = true   # true or false
base.name = "Port Wren (PWR)"    # text; shown on rosters
base.hotel_cap_usd = 189         # allowed 100-350 per night
base.crew_bus_headway_min = 25   # allowed 10-60
fatigue.risk_threshold = 0.72    # allowed 0.50-0.90 (score), above this triggers review
fatigue.night_duty_start = "22:00"  # 24-hour time
fatigue.night_duty_end = "06:00"    # 24-hour time
legal.contact = "ops-compliance@portwren.example"  # text

There are 21 settings here. I'll be changing roughly 6 of them each season.
